date.label: Undated thematic Leviticus legislation
date.note: This is a literary and thematic grouping in the Sinai narrative, not an independent datable event. No absolute year is inferred.

claims.claim: Leviticus 17 restricts blood consumption and relates blood to life and altar atonement.
claims.evidence: Lev 17:10–14; biblical theology stated by the text.

claims.claim: Leviticus 18 and 20 enumerate sexual prohibitions — alongside the Molech prohibition (18:21; 20:2–5), whose precise referent is disputed — and explain them in relation to communal and land holiness.
claims.evidence: Lev 18:1–30; 20:1–27; not mapped automatically to modern identity constructs.

claims.claim: Leviticus 19 commands care for neighbors, laborers, the poor and resident aliens alongside worship-related duties.
Leviticus 21–22 impose additional qualifications and regulations on priests, holy food, and offerings.
The term Holiness Code commonly refers to Leviticus 17–26, even though this page covers only 17–22.
claims.evidence: Lev 17–26 designation in Rhyder 2019, full JBL article on the Holiness legislation; Leviticus 17–22 direct text; Gnosis editorial segmentation is independent of common academic labeling.

claims.claim: Priestly and Holiness compositional layers, their sequence, and their dates remain scholarly reconstructions.
claims.evidence: Rhyder 2019 full article on H and sanctuary/Sabbath legislation; Ueoka 2018 full article on Holiness editorial festival theory (comparative context); these represent particular compositional proposals, not historically established dates.

claims.claim: Historical-critical scholars disagree over aspects of the ancient scope and social rationale of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13; that scholarly diversity is distinct from the received prohibition wording and from modern ethical conclusions.
claims.evidence: Stone 2022, Currents in Biblical Research 20(3) pp. 207–237; publisher metadata and author-hosted preprint directly inspected. Different scholarly proposals are reported, not treated as equally persuasive.

claims.claim: Holiness extends across sacred space, household, and civic life rather than dividing neatly into modern categories of religion and ethics.
claims.evidence: Lev 17–22; modern literary synthesis, not direct ancient sociology.

connections.note: A distinct legal account addresses slaughter and blood handling.
Social protections and wages recall care for vulnerable members in Leviticus 19.
Ezekiel 18:5–9 and 20 share legal concerns about individual responsibility and moral accountability.
A later priestly framework also concerns holiness, purity, and service.
Jesus directly cites Leviticus 19:18 as the command to love one’s neighbor.
The neighbor-love command is quoted in a Gospel dialogue.
Paul quotes Leviticus 19:18 in a summary of neighbor-oriented law.
James identifies the love-of-neighbor command as royal law.
Later Christian discussions of sexual morality require contextual interpretation, not identity of ancient and modern social categories.
